newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Sibneft seen thriving despite auction mystery.
newsitem.headline: Sibneft seen thriving despite auction mystery.

text.p: A senior Kremlin aide denied on Tuesday he had links to the mystery company which won control of Russia's seventh largest oil producer but analysts said Sibneft was primed to prosper in any case.

President Boris Yeltsin's security adviser Boris Berezovsky said he was not involved with OOO Finansovaya Neftyanaya Korporatsiya (FNK or Financial Oil Corp), the company which won control of Sibneft in an auction on Monday.
"I have no connection to FNK," Berezovsky told Reuters.
FNK won the tender for a controlling interest in Sibneft at the auction organised by Oil Financial Co (ZAO Neftyanaya Finansovaya Kompaniya or NFK) -- a separate company controlled by Berezovsky.
It offered a winning $110 million bid on a $101 million starting price, with commitments to pay another $100 million for the 51 percent stake.
MC Securities oil and gas director Stephen O'Sullivan said Sibneft's value was roughly $500-600 million.

A spokesman for Sibneft said he knew of no link between the coincidentally named FNK and NFK and that the auction winner was not controlled by Berezovsky. Sibneft said details of the FNK would be announced next week.
Oil analysts and market sources said there was no direct evidence that Berezovsky controlled the previously unknown FNK. The analysts said Sibneft could thrive with the auction over.
"The next issue will be consolidation of the Noyabrskneftegaz (production unit) and the Omsk refinery into Sibneft," said Dan Lubash, Merrill Lynch's managing director of emerging markets Europe.
"Both are among the highest quality oil assets in Russia."

Renaissance Capital investment bank oil analyst Alexei Kokin said Berezovsky appeared to have built up his stake in Sibneft by buying at cash auctions through intermediary companies over the last few years.
"The fact that there is one controlling owner allows him to share some of the equity without a big control loss risk, so they can pursue international equity placements."
Oil analysts said Berezovsky's group had not invested much in Sibneft and production unit Noyabrskneftegaz and some said consolidation could be risky for Noyabrsk investors.

Berezovsky's NFK had taken control of the Sibneft stake in 1995 under the controversial loans-for-shares programme, in which investors lent the government money in return for the right to manage state-owned stakes.
"If Sibneft wants to consolidate Noyabrsk, there is a high probability that it will do all it can to decrease the cost of Noyabrsk (shares)," Kokin said.
Sibneft is still threatened by Russia's third largest bank, Uneximbank, which promised to challenge the auction after its bid was disqualified by Berezovsky's group.
"Both entities are pretty strong and judging by Sidanko, (another dispute over an oil producer which has lasted years) it could draw out for a long time," said one analyst.
But foreign investors will soon forget about the messy auction, an unsurprising development in Russia, one industry source said.
"People are going to forget about the (auction) process two days from now," said the source, adding the winner would safely enjoy the results of a cheap acquisition.
